stem: Which paediatric fracture principle best explains why a child with a forearm injury is reviewed to check whether the bone has remained bowed rather than returned to its original position?

options.text: Young bones never bend before breaking
Long bones can bend substantially before cortical disruption and may undergo plastic bowing
All paediatric incomplete fractures are intra-articular
Children are more likely to dislocate than fracture
Compression forces usually cause spiral fractures at the physis

explanation: Long bones can bend substantially before cortical disruption and may undergo plastic bowing. This is why follow-up after a forearm injury includes checking for persistent bowing or incomplete return to alignment.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because young bones can bend before they break.
optionExplanations.B: Correct because paediatric long bones are more flexible and may sustain plastic deformation with bowing before cortical disruption.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because incomplete fractures are not inherently intra-articular; that description applies to epiphyseal injuries.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because children are more likely to sustain fractures than dislocations or sprains.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because compression is associated with buckle injury, particularly at the metaphysis, rather than spiral fracture at the physis.
